performers: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, baritone; Berlin Philharmonic; Rudolf Kempe, conductor
question: How does a repeated phrase change when its text moves from sunlight to personal grief?
intro: Rückert sets the rising sun against one parent’s private loss. Mahler answers with exposed oboe and horn lines, then lets the same small melodic cells pass between voice and orchestra.

sections.label: First stanza · sun and night
sections.mNote: oboe and horn establish the small melodic cells

sections.label: Second stanza · private loss
sections.mNote: opening outline varied for a new pair of lines

sections.label: Middle expansion · light
sections.mNote: familiar cells developed through a wider orchestral span

sections.label: Last stanza · the extinguished lamp
sections.mNote: opening material returns with altered text and accompaniment

cues.title: Two exposed lines
cues.text: The score opens with oboe and horn, not a full string chord. Their short rising steps and answering phrases provide material that the voice and other instruments can reshape throughout the song.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 3; an overview of the opening scoring, not a timestamped vocal entrance.

cues.title: A different accompaniment
cues.text: Across the first stanza, compare the bare wind writing with the harp and muted lower strings. The accompaniment changes colour while the vocal line continues to turn around small intervals.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 4–5. The report marks 0:36; relative level rises from −22.9 dB at 0:30 to −13.6 dB at 0:35. The instruments come from the score; placement is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A father’s poems
cues.text: Friedrich Rückert wrote the poems after two of his children died in 1833–34. Mahler chooses five from a much larger collection: the speaker’s private bereavement predates the composer’s own family.
cues.evidence: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/ The cycle’s textual origin, not a claim that Mahler experienced the events in the poem.

cues.title: Small steps, long sentences
cues.text: Listen across the phrases for two neighbouring notes moving by a semitone. Mahler joins these short cells into longer lines; the woodwind parts are often partners to the singer rather than a block of accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 3–8 show the recurrent neighbouring-note figures. This is a whole-song listening suggestion, not the identification of a particular note at this time.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Two composing summers
cues.text: Mahler works on the cycle in 1901 and 1904. Scholars disagree about which individual songs belong to each summer; the manuscript evidence does not justify assigning every song an exact composition date.
cues.evidence: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm Completion note distinguishes competing allocations of the five songs to 1901 and 1904.

cues.title: The middle grows outward
cues.text: The middle expansion enlarges the earlier material rather than replacing it with an unrelated tune. Higher string writing and a longer rise in intensity make the small opening figures occupy more space.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 10–14. The report changes at 2:58 and 3:04, then rises to its strongest windows around 3:20–3:45. The measurement supports the broad expansion, not an exact violin entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A sustained middle crest
cues.text: This stretch contains the recording’s strongest sustained rise. Follow the continuing phrase through its crest; a louder passage need not introduce a new melody.
cues.evidence: The analysis lists 3:20, 3:40 and 3:45 among the loudest five-second windows; it measures the contour without identifying orchestral parts.

cues.title: A baritone at the premiere
cues.text: Friedrich Weidemann sings the first performance in Vienna on 29 January 1905, with Mahler conducting. The venue is the Musikverein’s small hall, not its larger orchestral auditorium.
cues.evidence: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm Chronology and first-performance account identify singer, conductor, date and the Kleine Saal.

cues.title: Major does not erase minor
cues.text: Throughout the song, compare the minor-mode phrases with their major-mode inflections. The shift changes the colour of familiar notes without removing the poem’s opposition between a bright world and a bereaved parent.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 3–17 support the D-minor/D-major contrast. No key-estimation label is used to place a chord at this cue time.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Let the close settle
cues.text: The last phrase gives way to a short instrumental ending. Listen for the separated attacks and remaining resonance rather than treating the end of the sung sentence as the end of the song.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 17 supplies harp, glockenspiel and held wind tones after the final words. The report falls from −11.6 dB at 5:00 to −45.8 dB at 5:10; the precise vocal release is not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The opening returns with less preparation
transitions.how: The first stanza’s harp figures and bell-like punctuation leave space for a shortened return of the opening wind idea. The voice resumes the same melodic family with a changed rhythm, while flute and bassoon join the sparse texture. D minor remains the reference point: renewed counterpoint and changed words, rather than a new tonic or a full orchestral chord, distinguish the second statement.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 6–8. The report marks 1:24, with a quiet 1:25 window before the renewed rise at 1:35. This is a stanza-level estimate.

transitions.title: The small cells become a longer argument
transitions.how: The instrumental link develops the oboe’s neighbouring-note figures and passes the earlier vocal contour into the horns. When the voice continues, its line meets this material instead of repeating the opening accompaniment unchanged. First violins and harp subsequently widen the texture; the movement between D minor and major is worked through the existing motives.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 9–13. The 2:24 change and rising onset activity from 2:35 anchor the approximate start of the expanding middle. The written development, not machine key labels, supplies the formal interpretation.

transitions.title: The first gestures return after the crest
transitions.how: The expanded middle subsides into the opening’s short wind figures. The last stanza varies the first vocal contour, then restores the harp-and-string accompaniment as the text turns from the extinguished lamp towards the world’s light. Familiar melodic shapes hold the return together, while changed rhythm and scoring prevent a literal repeat.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 14–17. The report marks 3:52 after the 3:40–3:45 crest; level is −22.5 dB by 3:55. The timestamp does not identify the first syllable of the final stanza.

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song I, printed pp. 3–17; passage-level scoring, not an instantaneous list of sounding parts. Timings are provisional score proportions checked against the recording’s level changes; no bar alignment or aural verification.

timeline.note: Opening duet: oboe above the first horn; the voice and strings wait.
First-stanza passage: harp and muted lower strings replace the exposed opening duet.
The second stanza restores the wind-led texture; woodwind phrases answer the voice.
Middle expansion: the score introduces first violins into the upper melodic writing.
Returning wind figures surround the last stanza; the instrumental lines remain distinct.
In the later part of the restatement, harp and strings again carry the connected accompaniment.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
